title: A statistical-physics framework for translocation elastometry of deformable particles
abstract: A soft particle driven through a pore narrower than itself must deform to pass, and how quickly it does so is set by how hard it is to squeeze. We propose a mathematical framework for turning rate measurements of this driven, stochastic passage into quantitative mechanical measurements. Treating the entry of the particle as one-dimensional Brownian dynamics across an elastic barrier, we solve the transport problem exactly and identify two dynamical regimes: at low drive the passage is thermally activated and limited by the energy needed to deform the particle, and at high drive it is friction-limited. We propose a framework to extract the particle's deformation energy and relevant geometrical information by combining measurements in these two regimes. This method could be used in the context of nanopore sensing, where the drive is an applied voltage: the framework then provides a self-calibrating route---translocation elastometry---from a current-voltage measurement to the elasticity and shape of individual soft nanoparticles.
summary: This work presents a statistical physics framework to measure the elasticity and shape of soft nanoparticles by observing their translocation through a nanopore. It models the process using Brownian dynamics across an elastic barrier, deriving distinct velocity laws for low- and high-drive regimes. The key innovation is combining fits from both regimes to create a self-calibrating measurement that bypasses unknown experimental constants.
main_problem: To develop a mathematical framework that converts rate measurements of a soft particle passing through a narrow pore into quantitative mechanical characterization of the particle's deformation energy and geometry.
main_result: By combining measurements from both low-drive (activated) and high-drive (frictional) regimes, the method achieves a self-calibrating readout to determine the dimensionless deformation energy ($\Delta/k_B T$) without needing to know the unknown force-to-voltage conversion factor.
method: The problem is solved exactly by analyzing the steady-state Fokker–Planck equation governing one-dimensional over-damped Brownian dynamics across an elastic barrier, identifying distinct dynamical regimes based on applied drive strength.
model_or_system: The system models a deformable soft particle translocating through a pore using a 'funnel model' potential. The dynamics are governed by the Langevin equation, analyzed via its steady-state probability flux.
key_observables: Mean translocation velocity ($v$), deformation energy ($\Delta/k_B T$), funnel length ($L_f$), and crossover force ($\psi_c$).
important_parameters: Deformation energy ($\Delta$), pore geometry parameter ($L_f$), applied driving force ($\psi$), and thermal energy scale ($k_B T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the drive is constant, the process can be reduced to a single reaction coordinate (one-dimensional dynamics), and initially models the elastic potential as piecewise linear.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the one-dimensional potential landscape, the master velocity curve showing distinct regimes (linear/activated), and phase diagrams mapping these dynamical regions in parameter space.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model via the Langevin equation, solves the resulting Fokker-Planck equation to derive analytical expressions for velocity in different drive regimes, and then proposes a dual-readout fitting procedure that combines linear (frictional) and exponential (activated) fits to eliminate unknown constants.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (Fokker-Planck formalism) to extract mechanical parameters from time-dependent current measurements is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems where dissipation and thermal fluctuations dominate the dynamics.
